thread.title: Earnings worries weigh on Asian markets; China suffers worst week since 2016

author: morningstar.com
title: Earnings worries weigh on Asian markets; China suffers worst week since 2016
text:
By Lucy Craymer
Samsung falls on outlook uncertainty
Stock indexes in Japan and South Korea suffered earnings-related hits Friday, with Samsung Electronics falling more than 4% after rival Apple's latest quarterly financial results.
Meanwhile, China's benchmark index logges its biggest weekly loss since 2016, with fresh concerns about Beijing's campaign to cut financial risk and predictions of a slowing economy helping erase half of the market's year-to-date gains in just a few days.
Apple (AAPL) reported a slight drop in iPhone sales in the three months through December and gave a downbeat revenue forecast for the current quarter. Its shares still rose 3.4% in after-hours trading as the tech giant's overall results beat expectations and because the stock's performance had been lackluster for several months on worries about demand for the iPhone X.

(http://www.marketwatch.com/story/apple-earnings-show-iphone-supercycle-isnt-happening-and-thats-ok-2018-02-01)Plus: Apple has $163 billion to burn, and Tim Cook plans to spend it (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/apple-has-163-billion-to-burn-and-tim-cook-plans-to-spend-it-2018-02-01)
Samsung (005930.SE), down 4.3%, has its own line of smartphones but also makes various phone components including chips and screens. "The market is concerned about the uncertainty" surrounding Samsung's outlook, said S.K. Kim, an analyst at Daiwa Capital Markets. Chip maker SK Hynix (000660.SE) dropped 3%, contributing to the Kospi's 1.7% decline.
Japan's Nikkei Stock Average , closed down 0.9% following earnings-related news. Airline ANA Holdings (9202.TO) and investment bank Nomura Holdings (8604.TO) reported results after the bell Thursday, and their shares fell 4.1% and 2.9%, respectively.
Chinese stocks erased an earlier loss to close up 0.4%, but still ended down 2.7% for the week, the biggest weekly loss since December 2016. The weakness came on the back of local data this week that showed China's manufacturing-sector growth slowed in January. In addition, the People's Bank of China has drained money from the financial system via open-market operations for six consecutive days.
Rob Carnell, chief economist and head of research for Asia-Pacific at ING in Singapore, said investors will be looking to service-sector data next week for sign of slowness there. "If the services are holding up OK, then the markets won't be that upset about manufacturing looking soft because it would show the shift from manufacturing to services and consumer spending."
The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield nearly reached 2.8% in Asian trading and was at four-year highs. The WSJ Dollar Index was recently up 0.3%, while S&P 500 futures fell 0.6% as traders looked ahead to the closely watched U.S. jobs report. The data come out at 8:30 a.m. Eastern Time.
In India, where the government released its budget for the coming fiscal year on Thursday, the Sensex benchmark ended down 2.3% as investors weigh the reintroduction of a capital-gains tax.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 climbed 0.5%, boosted by a 2.4% jump in the energy sector, that group's best day in three months. Oil futures were higher during Australian trading hours with crude at $66.11 a barrel. ANZ Bank said the market's focus has returned to the positive macroeconomic backdrop, looking past record levels of U.S. oil production.
Bitcoin prices fell further in Asia (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/no-letup-for-bitcoin-as-cryptocurrency-drops-further-below-9000-2018-02-02), approaching $8,500, according to CoinDesk, about 15% below levels from 24 hours earlier. The volatile cryptocurrency is at levels last seen in late November.
-Lucy Craymer ; 02-18 0627ET
